Materialism. The philosophical position that all that exists is ultimately physical matter—its arrangements and interactions—with no immaterial substances or properties. It directly opposes dualism by rejecting any separate mind or soul distinct from the body. Materialism underpins much of modern science and philosophy of mind, though it faces a persistent challenge: explaining subjective experience.

The materialist claims that all phenomena, including thought and consciousness, can be reduced to or explained by physical processes. There is no soul, spirit, or immaterial mind. This view is often paired with mechanism—the idea that all causation reduces to physical laws and forces governing matter and its arrangements.

The ancient atomists, especially Democritus, argued that only atoms and void are real. This was an early form of materialism rejected by Plato and Aristotle. Centuries later, Marxist materialism applied the doctrine to history: material economic conditions and relations of production shape social consciousness, culture, and institutions.

But materialism faces acute challenges, most notably the hard problem of consciousness. How do physical processes in the brain produce subjective experience—qualia—rather than proceeding mechanically in the dark? Contemporary versions like physicalism and functionalism attempt to accommodate mental states, intentionality, and meaning within a strictly materialist framework, yet the explanatory gap persists. Even if we map all neural correlates of consciousness, it remains unclear how objective physical processes generate subjective felt experience.

Materialism connects to dualism, its opposite position, which claims immaterial mind exists alongside physical body. It also relates to consciousness, the greatest challenge for materialism, and to the mind-body problem itself—the foundational puzzle materialism attempts to solve by reducing mental phenomena to physical brain processes. Qualia, the subjective qualities of experience that resist reduction to physical properties, pose the hardest problem for the materialist view. Marxism applies materialist principles to history and political economy. Finally, panpsychism offers an alternative by attributing consciousness or consciousness-like properties to fundamental matter, solving the hard problem differently from materialism's standard approach.
